1.title: Why Roman law is taught first — purpose of the series
1.text: Gamauf opens Part 1 of the JAP series 'Basics des römischen Rechts' by explaining why law students start with Roman law. From the first semester they are meant to learn basic structures of private law that are still effective today and — starting from the EXEGESIS of Digest texts — to develop the skill of solving legal cases. Roman law is didactically especially suitable because the Roman jurists usually do NOT lay out a case in its full complexity: they isolate ONE aspect and discuss it thoroughly. Concentrating on the aspect the jurist singled out allows demanding discussion from the very first class without having to chase every ramification of the case, as a problem of modern law would require. Step by step students learn the building blocks of the law of property and obligations ('Vermögensprivatrecht') and later understand the Roman-influenced rules of the ABGB better. Although the course is mainly propaedeutic and case-oriented, it cannot do without legal-historical background: the sources of law, the role of legal science and the genres of legal literature. The importance of Roman law for European private law can only be grasped by someone who knows Justinian's legislative work; modern jurisprudence stands in a tradition that sprang from the constant engagement with the CORPUS IURIS CIVILIS from the Middle Ages to the 19th century, and what unites and separates modern European codifications is visible only through the RECEPTION of Roman law. Footnotes: the Vienna subject is therefore called 'Romanistische Fundamente europäischer Privatrechte und Technik der Falllösung'; the series plan is Part 1 = sources of law, Part 2 = legal science and legal literature, Part 3 = Justinian's compilations and the reception. The article says this knowledge is presupposed in the FÜM I exam. For your exegesis: the jurist's habit of isolating one aspect is exactly what you exploit — identify the one legal problem he discusses.

terms.def: Structured interpretation and commentary of a Digest text; in Vienna the starting point for learning to solve cases.
Later name for Justinian's legislative compilations (528–534 AD), which preserved the achievements of Roman jurisprudence.
The adoption of Roman law in Europe from the Middle Ages on — the key process for understanding what links and divides modern European codifications.

cards.q: Why is Roman law didactically suitable for learning to solve cases, according to Gamauf?
cards.a:
Roman jurists usually do not set out a case in its full complexity but isolate ONE aspect and discuss it thoroughly.
• This allows serious discussion from the first class.
• Students need not follow every ramification of the case as in a modern-law problem (no overload).
• Step by step one learns the building blocks of property and obligations law.

cards.q: Which legal-historical background knowledge does the Roman-law course need despite being mainly case-oriented?
cards.a:
The basic structural elements that make work with classical sources fruitful:
• the sources of law
• the role of legal science (jurisprudence)
• the genres of legal literature

cards.q: Why does a modern lawyer need to know Justinian's legislation and the reception, according to Gamauf?
cards.a:
Because modern European jurisprudence grew out of the engagement with the CORPUS IURIS CIVILIS from the Middle Ages to the 19th century.
• Roman law's role as driving force of European private law is visible only to those who know Justinian's work.
• What unites and separates modern European codifications can only be seen through the RECEPTION.

cards.q: How are the three parts of Gamauf's 'Basics des römischen Rechts' divided?
cards.a: Part 1: sources of law · Part 2: legal science (jurisprudence) and legal literature · Part 3: Justinian's compilations and the reception.

cards.q: What does the habit of Roman jurists to isolate one aspect of a case mean for writing an exegesis?
cards.a:
Find the ONE legal problem the jurist singles out and build the analysis around it.
• The article: concentrating on the aspect highlighted by the jurist is what makes Digest exegesis workable for beginners.
• You do not have to solve every possible side issue of the facts.

2.title: Periodisation: about 1,000 years of ancient Roman law
2.text: The development of Roman law in antiquity spans roughly 1,000 YEARS. It becomes historically tangible as a private-law order for the first time in the TWELVE TABLES, conventionally dated 451/450 BC. The end point is the compilation of what was later called the CORPUS IURIS CIVILIS between 528 and 534 AD, which preserved the achievements of Roman jurisprudence for posterity. Roman legal science was especially productive from the END OF THE 1ST CENTURY BC to the END OF THE 3RD CENTURY AD; this period is usually called CLASSICAL Roman jurisprudence and CLASSICAL law. (Note: Part 2 of the same series dates the classical period from the 1st century BC to the FIRST THIRD of the 3rd century AD.) The post-ancient engagement with Roman law has lasted roughly ANOTHER 1,000 YEARS, since its beginnings at the University of BOLOGNA in the 11TH CENTURY. Without the rediscovered Corpus iuris civilis there would have been no reception, no European legal science and its IUS COMMUNE (common law), and no national CODIFICATIONS rooted in it from the late 18th century. Footnote 5: the term 'classical' became established in 19th-century historiography for periods whose achievements posterity regards as outstanding and authoritative (Greek sculpture, Weimar classicism, Viennese classical music); Gamauf warns that such evaluative periodisation does not help to understand historical developments.

terms.def: Most productive phase of Roman legal science, end of 1st c. BC – end of 3rd c. AD (Part 1); 'classical law' is the law of this period.
The common European law created by legal science on the basis of the rediscovered Corpus iuris civilis.

cards.q: Which two events frame the roughly 1,000-year development of ancient Roman law?
cards.a:
Start: the TWELVE TABLES, dated 451/450 BC — first tangible private-law order.
End: the compilation of the CORPUS IURIS CIVILIS, 528–534 AD.

cards.q: Which period does Gamauf (Part 1) call 'classical' Roman jurisprudence?
cards.a:
End of the 1st century BC to the end of the 3rd century AD — the most productive phase of Roman legal science.
• Part 2 of the series dates it slightly differently: 1st c. BC to the first third of the 3rd c. AD.

cards.q: When and where did the post-ancient study of Roman law begin, and how long has it lasted?
cards.a: At the University of BOLOGNA in the 11th century — roughly another 1,000 years.

cards.q: What would not have happened without the rediscovered Corpus iuris civilis, according to Gamauf?
cards.a:
• the RECEPTION of Roman law
• a European legal science and its IUS COMMUNE
• the national CODIFICATIONS rooted in it from the late 18th century

cards.q: What is Gamauf's criticism of the label 'classical'?
cards.a: It is an evaluative term (established in the 19th century for periods considered outstanding) and such evaluative periodisation does not help to understand historical developments.

3.title: Layers of the Roman legal order (Rechtsschichten)
3.text: The Roman legal order is described in LAYERS (Rechtsschichten), but these were NOT hierarchical like the modern 'Stufenbau' of norms. A term gets its specific meaning only in CONTRAST to another layer. (1) IUS CIVILE vs IUS GENTIUM: ius civile is the genuinely national Roman law, applicable ONLY to Roman citizens, insofar as it deviates from the norms of IUS GENTIUM accepted by all civilised peoples. Example (fn 6): derivative acquisition of ownership by MANCIPATIO was open only to Roman citizens, whereas TRADITIO was open also to a PEREGRINUS. Assigning a rule to ius gentium did NOT mean it was borrowed from a foreign legal order — it reflected the observation that the rule also existed in other political communities, which was not the case for old civil institutions such as PATRIA POTESTAS. (2) IUS CIVILE vs IUS HONORARIUM: in a perspective limited to Rome, ius civile means the law based on the Twelve Tables, custom and legislation, opposed to the IUS HONORARIUM created by the PRAETOR. Example (fn 7): civil ownership protected by the REI VINDICATIO comes from ius civile; BONITARY ownership enforceable by the ACTIO PUBLICIANA is honorary law. In the sense of the ius civile – ius gentium dichotomy, however, the ius honorarium was itself part of the ius civile. (3) IUS NATURALE: some jurists saw it as the basis of ius gentium, but ius gentium could displace it. Fn 8: by ius naturale all men are free (cf. § 16 ABGB); SLAVERY, contradicting that freedom, was seen as a product of ius gentium (Ulp. D. 1,1,4). Acquisition of ownership could rest on ius civile (MANCIPATIO, USUCAPIO), on ius gentium (TRADITIO, OCCUPATIO of war booty) or on ius naturale (natural modes of acquisition). (4) IUS PUBLICUM vs IUS PRIVATUM: Ulpian used these terms only to characterise different areas (Ulp. D. 1,1,1,2), not to introduce a theoretical distinction in the modern sense. Ius publicum, as IUS COGENS, could not be changed by private agreement (the article cites 'Pap. D. 1,1,1,2' — apparently a misprint, since that is the Ulpian passage; the well-known Papinian dictum stands in D. 2,14,38). But private-law norms were by no means always IUS DISPOSITIVUM.

terms.def: (a) Genuinely Roman law applicable only to Roman citizens, as opposed to ius gentium; (b) law based on the Twelve Tables, custom and legislation, as opposed to ius honorarium.
Norms accepted by all civilised peoples; a rule was so classified because it also existed elsewhere, not because it was borrowed.
Law created by the praetor's jurisdictional activity; supplements or overlays ius civile.
Natural law; for some jurists the basis of ius gentium, but displaceable by it (all men free by nature; slavery from ius gentium).
Mandatory law that private agreement cannot change; ius publicum was ius cogens.
Law that the parties may derogate from by agreement; private-law norms were not always dispositive.
Praetorian ('in bonis') ownership protected by the ACTIO PUBLICIANA, as opposed to civil ownership protected by the REI VINDICATIO.
A free non-citizen; could use institutions of ius gentium such as traditio but not mancipatio.

cards.q: How did the Roman 'layers of law' differ from the modern hierarchy of norms?
cards.a:
They were NOT hierarchical (no 'Stufenbau').
• A term got its specific meaning only in contrast to another layer.

cards.q: Distinguish IUS CIVILE and IUS GENTIUM.
cards.a:
IUS CIVILE = genuinely Roman law, applicable only to Roman citizens, insofar as it deviates from IUS GENTIUM.
• IUS GENTIUM = norms accepted by all civilised peoples.
• Example: MANCIPATIO only for citizens (ius civile); TRADITIO also for a PEREGRINUS (ius gentium).

cards.q: Did classifying a rule as IUS GENTIUM mean the Romans had borrowed it from a foreign legal order?
cards.a:
No. It reflected the observation that the rule also existed in other political communities.
• Old civil institutions such as PATRIA POTESTAS did not exist elsewhere and therefore were ius civile.

cards.q: Distinguish IUS CIVILE and IUS HONORARIUM.
cards.a:
In a perspective limited to Rome: IUS CIVILE = law based on the Twelve Tables, custom and legislation; IUS HONORARIUM = law created by the PRAETOR.
• Example: civil ownership (REI VINDICATIO) vs BONITARY ownership (ACTIO PUBLICIANA).

cards.q: Which remedy protects civil ownership and which protects bonitary ownership, and which legal layer does each belong to?
cards.a:
Civil ownership: REI VINDICATIO — IUS CIVILE.
Bonitary ownership: ACTIO PUBLICIANA — IUS HONORARIUM.

cards.q: In the ius civile – ius gentium dichotomy, where does the IUS HONORARIUM belong?
cards.a: It is part of the IUS CIVILE — the meaning of 'ius civile' depends on which layer it is contrasted with.

cards.q: How did the Roman jurists relate IUS NATURALE and IUS GENTIUM, using slavery as the example?
cards.a:
Some jurists saw IUS NATURALE as the basis of IUS GENTIUM, but ius gentium could displace it.
• By ius naturale all men are free (cf. § 16 ABGB).
• SLAVERY contradicts this and was regarded as a product of ius gentium (Ulp. D. 1,1,4).

cards.q: On which legal layer does each mode of acquiring ownership rest, according to the Roman jurists?
cards.a:
• IUS CIVILE: MANCIPATIO, USUCAPIO
• IUS GENTIUM: TRADITIO, OCCUPATIO of war booty
• IUS NATURALE: the natural modes of acquisition

cards.q: What did Ulpian mean by IUS PUBLICUM and IUS PRIVATUM (D. 1,1,1,2)?
cards.a:
He used the terms only to characterise different areas of law — not as a theoretical distinction in the modern sense.
• Ius publicum was IUS COGENS: not changeable by private agreement.
• Private-law norms were nevertheless not always IUS DISPOSITIVUM.

cards.q: Was Roman private law always IUS DISPOSITIVUM?
cards.a: No. Ius publicum was ius cogens, but that does not mean private-law norms were always dispositive.

4.title: The Twelve Tables
4.text: The Romans regarded the TWELVE TABLES as the starting point of their law. Because early Roman history is often unclear (uncertain sources, contradictions, contamination with later misunderstandings), the very existence of this legislation has repeatedly been doubted since the 17TH CENTURY. Roman authors placed it in the context of the STRUGGLE OF THE ORDERS between PATRICIANS and PLEBEIANS: according to tradition, in 451 BC a special legislative commission of TEN MEN drafted TEN tables; a further commission added TWO more the following year. Content and purposes: the Twelve Tables were NOT a comprehensive codification but mainly regulated DISPUTED QUESTIONS; in particular they set MINIMUM STANDARDS TO PROTECT THE SOCIALLY WEAKER (e.g. summons to court, enforcement law). They LIMITED PRIVATE REVENGE — for bodily injury it gave way to the TALIO principle, with the possibility of replacing actual retaliation by MONEY — and they show the FIRST ATTEMPT TO GRASP NEGLIGENCE conceptually. Transmission: modern reconstructions rest on mostly NON-LITERAL quotations in later literary and legal authors (latest collection: Flach 2004). Reception in antiquity: CICERO (1st c. BC) claimed to have learned them by heart as a child and valued them above Greek philosophy; LIVY (under Augustus) glorified them — unjustifiably — as the source of all 'public and private law'; GAIUS still wrote a commentary on them in the 2nd century AD; until Justinian jurists stressed the venerability of a rule by tracing it back to the Twelve Tables.

terms.def: Legislation dated 451/450 BC; starting point of Roman law in Roman eyes; not a comprehensive code.
Retaliation in kind; in the Twelve Tables it replaced unlimited private revenge for bodily injury and could be bought off with money.
Conflict between patricians and plebeians in the early Republic; Roman authors placed the Twelve Tables in this context.

cards.q: What purposes did the Twelve Tables serve? (Kontrollfrage)
cards.a:
They mainly settled DISPUTED QUESTIONS — not a comprehensive codification.
• Minimum standards protecting the socially weaker (summons to court, enforcement)
• Limiting private revenge: TALIO for bodily injury, replaceable by money
• First attempt to grasp negligence conceptually

cards.q: How did the Twelve Tables come about according to Roman tradition?
cards.a:
As a result of the struggle of the orders (patricians vs plebeians):
451 BC commission of ten men → ten tables → next year a further commission → two more tables.

cards.q: Were the Twelve Tables a comprehensive codification?
cards.a: No — they mainly regulated disputed questions and set minimum standards in some areas.

cards.q: How did the Twelve Tables treat private revenge for bodily injury?
cards.a: They limited it: revenge gave way to the TALIO principle, and actual retaliation could be replaced by a money payment.

cards.q: On what are modern reconstructions of the Twelve Tables based, and since when has their existence been doubted?
cards.a:
On mostly non-literal quotations in later literary and legal authors (latest collection Flach 2004).
• Their existence has repeatedly been doubted since the 17th century.

cards.q: How did Cicero, Livy and Gaius relate to the Twelve Tables?
cards.a:
• CICERO: claimed to have learned them by heart as a child; valued them above Greek philosophy.
• LIVY (under Augustus): glorified them (unjustifiably) as the source of all public and private law.
• GAIUS: wrote a commentary on them in the 2nd century AD.

cards.q: Why did jurists until Justinian trace rules back to the Twelve Tables?
cards.a: To emphasise the venerability (dignity, authority) of those rules.

5.title: Legislation of the Republic: LEX, PLEBISCITUM, popular assemblies
5.text: The Twelve Tables form the basis of the IUS CIVILE, which in the Republic was developed first by the PONTIFICAL JURISPRUDENCE and later by secular legal science. FORMAL LEGISLATION played only a SUBORDINATE role for private law. A statute (LEX PUBLICA) was passed by the POPULAR ASSEMBLY and named after its proposer(s); double names such as the LEX PAPIA POPPAEA show the two CONSULS as joint proposers (fn 11). Republican statutes reacted AD HOC to current problems and mostly had only marginal significance for private law (e.g. various sumptuary/luxury laws). From the LEX HORTENSIA of 287 BC the PLEBISCITA — resolutions of the special assemblies of the plebs (CONCILIA PLEBIS) passed on the motion of a TRIBUNE OF THE PLEBS — were equal to statutes; therefore they were also called LEX (e.g. LEX AQUILIA). Fn 10: the Roman people could meet in differently organised assemblies; statutes were passed mainly by the COMITIA CENTURIATA, whose structure derived from the army. All male citizens voted, but only the votes of the few rich were decisive, because they could afford the more expensive equipment and formed the core of the army. Certain MAGISTRATES could propose statutes; the assembly could only ACCEPT or REJECT them, not amend them.

terms.def: Statute passed by a popular assembly on a magistrate's proposal; named after the proposer(s).
Resolution of the CONCILIUM PLEBIS on the motion of a tribune of the plebs; equal to a lex since the LEX HORTENSIA (287 BC).
Special assemblies of the plebs.
Main law-making assembly, organised on the army structure; the rich minority's votes were decisive.
287 BC: made plebiscita equal to statutes.

cards.q: What role did formal legislation play for Roman private law in the Republic?
cards.a:
Only a subordinate one.
• The ius civile was developed mainly by pontifical, later secular jurisprudence.
• Republican statutes reacted ad hoc to current problems, mostly marginal for private law (e.g. sumptuary laws).

cards.q: Why is the LEX AQUILIA called a 'lex' although it was a plebiscite?
cards.a: Since the LEX HORTENSIA (287 BC) plebiscita passed in the CONCILIA PLEBIS on a tribune's motion were equal to statutes, so they too were called LEX.

cards.q: In which year were plebiscita made equal to statutes, and by which law?
cards.a: 287 BC, by the LEX HORTENSIA.

cards.q: Distinguish a LEX PUBLICA from a PLEBISCITUM.
cards.a:
LEX PUBLICA: passed by the popular assembly (mainly COMITIA CENTURIATA) on a magistrate's proposal.
PLEBISCITUM: passed by the assembly of the plebs (CONCILIUM PLEBIS) on the motion of a tribune of the plebs; equal to a lex from 287 BC.

cards.q: How was a Roman statute named, and what does a double name like LEX PAPIA POPPAEA show?
cards.a: After its proposer(s); a double name shows the two consuls as joint proposers.

cards.q: What could the popular assembly do with a magistrate's legislative proposal?
cards.a: Only accept or reject it — it could not amend it.

cards.q: Why were the votes of the rich decisive in the COMITIA CENTURIATA?
cards.a: Its structure derived from the army: the rich could provide the more expensive equipment and formed the core of the army, which explains their voting weight.

6.title: The praetor and his edict — IUS HONORARIUM
6.text: From the 3RD CENTURY BC extensive conquests brought economic and social change: Roman society shed the agrarian character presupposed by the Twelve Tables, which required private-law reform. In Rome this task was taken on NOT by legislation but by a judicial official, the PRAETOR. The praetorship was the SECOND-HIGHEST office of the developed republican constitution (fn 12: in other Italian constitutions the praetor — literally 'prae-itor', the one who goes ahead — held the highest office); its main field was the administration of justice. As a magistrate he held IMPERIUM and the IUS EDICENDI (fn 13). In the FORMULARY PROCEDURE the praetor examined at the start (IN IURE) ABSTRACTLY whether a recognised remedy existed for the plaintiff's claim and then left the concrete decision to a LAY JUDGE / IUDEX (APUD IUDICEM). Each new praetor published at the start of his year of office an EDICT listing the remedies he intended to grant (ACTIONES, EXCEPTIONES, INTERDICTA …). A core stock soon remained the same from year to year (EDICTUM TRALATICIUM), supplemented by occasional innovations (NOVAE CLAUSULAE). The praetor could also grant AD HOC protection not foreseen in the edict, e.g. by an ACTIO IN FACTUM or ACTIO UTILIS. In this way the IUS HONORARIUM / PRAETORIUM arose — a layer that partly SUPPLEMENTS the ius civile (e.g. actiones in factum to the LEX AQUILIA) and partly OVERLAYS it with new institutions (e.g. BONITARY OWNERSHIP, praetorian succession law). Expansion also increased legal dealings with PEREGRINES; in 242 BC a PRAETOR PEREGRINUS was appointed. In dealings with peregrines, alternatives to the old civil formal acts derived from ius gentium were first used (e.g. TRADITIO instead of MANCIPATIO) and then entered the edict of the now so-called PRAETOR URBANUS. On Emperor HADRIAN's order the jurist JULIAN made the final redaction around 130 AD — the EDICTUM PERPETUUM (reconstructed by Lenel, 3rd ed. 1927). The edict thereby had its final form, the praetors lost any further power to develop the law, and this power was concentrated in the EMPEROR. Julian also gave its final form to the EDICT OF THE CURULE AEDILES on the market sale of SLAVES and DRAUGHT ANIMALS, which first provided WARRANTY FOR DEFECTS INDEPENDENT OF FAULT. Fn 14: until the CONSTITUTIO ANTONINIANA of 212 AD inhabitants of the empire were divided into Romans and peregrines; peregrines in principle lived by their local laws, known mainly from Egypt through legal papyrology.

terms.def: Second-highest republican magistrate, responsible for the administration of justice; creator of the ius honorarium.
The praetor's power of command as magistrate / his right to issue edicts.

terms.term: Formulary procedure: IN IURE / APUD IUDICEM
terms.def: Two stages: before the praetor (abstract check whether a remedy exists) and before the lay judge (IUDEX), who decides the concrete case.
The core of the edict carried over unchanged from year to year.
Occasional new clauses added to the edict.
Remedies the praetor could grant ad hoc beyond the edict (e.g. actiones in factum supplementing the lex Aquilia).
Praetor for dealings with peregrines (from 242 BC) / the city praetor, whose edict took over ius-gentium alternatives such as traditio.
Final redaction of the praetorian edict by Julian on Hadrian's order, c. 130 AD; ended praetorian law-making.
Rules on the market sale of slaves and draught animals; first provided strict (fault-independent) warranty for defects; final form by Julian.

cards.q: How was the Roman private-law order adapted to new requirements in the Republic? (Kontrollfrage)
cards.a:
Not by legislation but through the PRAETOR's edict and remedies → IUS HONORARIUM.
• Trigger: conquests from the 3rd c. BC changed the agrarian society of the Twelve Tables.
• Annual edict listing ACTIONES, EXCEPTIONES, INTERDICTA; ad hoc ACTIO IN FACTUM / ACTIO UTILIS.
• PRAETOR PEREGRINUS (242 BC): ius-gentium alternatives such as TRADITIO, later taken into the urban edict.
• (Also: interpretation by pontifical and secular jurisprudence, Part 2.)

cards.q: Describe the two stages of the formulary procedure.
cards.a:
IN IURE: the praetor examines abstractly whether a recognised remedy exists for the plaintiff's claim.
APUD IUDICEM: a lay judge (IUDEX) decides the concrete case.

cards.q: What did the praetor's edict contain and when was it published?
cards.a: The remedies he intended to grant (ACTIONES, EXCEPTIONES, INTERDICTA …); each new praetor published it at the start of his year of office.

cards.q: Distinguish EDICTUM TRALATICIUM and NOVAE CLAUSULAE.
cards.a:
EDICTUM TRALATICIUM = core stock carried over unchanged year after year.
NOVAE CLAUSULAE = occasional innovations added to it.

cards.q: In which two ways does the IUS HONORARIUM relate to the IUS CIVILE? Give an example of each.
cards.a:
• SUPPLEMENTING it — e.g. ACTIONES IN FACTUM to the LEX AQUILIA.
• OVERLAYING it with new institutions — e.g. BONITARY OWNERSHIP, praetorian succession law.

cards.q: Which rank did the praetorship have in the republican constitution?
cards.a: The second-highest office; main task the administration of justice. (In other Italian constitutions the praetor — 'prae-itor', the one who goes ahead — was the highest office.)

cards.q: When was the PRAETOR PEREGRINUS appointed and why?
cards.a: 242 BC — because Roman expansion increased legal dealings with peregrines.

cards.q: How did TRADITIO enter the praetorian edict as a substitute for MANCIPATIO?
cards.a: In dealings with peregrines, alternatives derived from IUS GENTIUM were first applied (TRADITIO instead of MANCIPATIO) and then entered the edict of the PRAETOR URBANUS.

cards.q: Who made the final redaction of the praetorian edict, when, and with what consequence?
cards.a:
The jurist JULIAN on Emperor HADRIAN's order, c. 130 AD → EDICTUM PERPETUUM.
• The edict got its final form.
• Praetors lost the power to develop the law; it was concentrated in the emperor.

cards.q: What was special about the edict of the curule aediles?
cards.a: It regulated the market sale of slaves and draught animals and for the first time provided warranty for defects INDEPENDENT OF FAULT; Julian gave it its final form.

cards.q: Until when were the inhabitants of the empire divided into Romans and peregrines, and by what law did peregrines live?
cards.a: Until the CONSTITUTIO ANTONINIANA of 212 AD; peregrines lived in principle by their local laws (known mainly from Egypt via legal papyrology).

cards.q: Which two powers did the praetor hold as a magistrate?
cards.a: IMPERIUM (power of command) and the IUS EDICENDI (right to issue edicts).

7.title: SENATUS CONSULTA and the ORATIO PRINCIPIS
7.text: The monarchy founded by AUGUSTUS tended from the start to subject law-making to imperial control. Legislation in the popular assembly soon fell out of use; instead the SENATE became the legislator. In the Republic a SENATUS CONSULTUM was — as the name says — only a legally NON-BINDING ADVICE to the highest magistrates, though it was opportune for them to take seriously the will of the politically and economically leading men gathered there. In the 1ST CENTURY AD senatus consulta also formally obtained the FORCE OF LAW; examples important for private law are the SC MACEDONIANUM and the SC VELLEIANUM. However, the Senate lost its autonomy and adapted so far to the emperor's wishes that its formal resolution finally became dispensable: from the END OF THE 2ND CENTURY the emperor's legislative motion, the ORATIO PRINCIPIS, by itself already had the character of a source of law.

terms.def: Resolution of the Senate; in the Republic non-binding advice to the magistrates, from the 1st c. AD formally with force of law.
The emperor's legislative motion to the Senate; from the end of the 2nd c. AD a source of law by itself.
Examples of senatus consulta important for private law.

cards.q: How did the legal force of a SENATUS CONSULTUM change from the Republic to the Principate?
cards.a:
Republic: legally non-binding advice to the highest magistrates (politically opportune to follow).
1st c. AD: formally obtained force of law.

cards.q: How did the ORATIO PRINCIPIS obtain force of law? (Kontrollfrage)
cards.a:
The Senate lost its autonomy and adapted to the emperor's wishes so far that its formal resolution became dispensable.
• From the end of the 2nd century AD the emperor's motion (ORATIO PRINCIPIS) alone was a source of law.

cards.q: Name two senatus consulta important for private law mentioned by Gamauf.
cards.a: SC MACEDONIANUM and SC VELLEIANUM.

cards.q: Which body replaced the popular assembly as legislator under Augustus' monarchy?
cards.a: The SENATE — legislation in the popular assembly fell out of use.

8.title: CONSTITUTIONES PRINCIPIS — imperial legislation and the rescript
8.text: Imperial legislation took place mainly through CONSTITUTIONES PRINCIPIS (imperial constitutions). The collective term covered EDICTA issued by the emperor as magistrate, his MANDATA (service instructions to subordinate officials) and his DECRETA (judgments in proceedings of first or second instance). The MOST IMPORTANT form, however, was the RESCRIPTUM. Like a jurist's RESPONSUM, a rescript contained the SOLUTION OF A LEGAL QUESTION, NOT the decision of an actual case. Officials or private persons could submit a query and ask for the emperor's legal opinion on the facts they reported. The concrete judgment could follow the rescript IF the facts assumed in it were PROVEN. Initially rescripts interpreted the existing law for the individual case; after the final redaction of the edict they increasingly had a LAW-CREATING effect and were observed beyond the concrete case. They were drafted in specialised chanceries — AB EPISTULIS (queries from officials) and A LIBELLIS (queries from private persons) — often headed by important jurists; but the emperor kept the last word over their proposals. Fn 16: structural similarity to the PRELIMINARY RULING of the CJEU under Art 267 TFEU: the Court answers the question of EU law put to it, and the national body then decides the concrete case on that basis (Winkel 2007).

terms.def: Collective term for imperial legislation: EDICTA, MANDATA, DECRETA, RESCRIPTA.
General enactment issued by the emperor as magistrate.
Service instruction of the emperor to a subordinate official.
The emperor's judgment in a trial of first or second instance.
The emperor's answer to a legal query on reported facts; most important form of imperial constitution.
Imperial chanceries for queries from officials / from private persons.

cards.q: Which four forms fell under the term CONSTITUTIONES PRINCIPIS?
cards.a:
• EDICTA — enactments of the emperor as magistrate
• MANDATA — service instructions to subordinate officials
• DECRETA — judgments in first or second instance
• RESCRIPTA — answers to legal queries (the most important form)

cards.q: What did a RESCRIPTUM and a jurist's RESPONSUM have in common?
cards.a:
Both contained the solution of a LEGAL QUESTION on the facts reported, not the decision of an actual case.
• The judge could follow it only if the facts assumed were proven.

cards.q: Distinguish a RESCRIPTUM from a DECRETUM.
cards.a:
RESCRIPTUM: legal opinion on facts reported in a query — no decision of the case itself.
DECRETUM: the emperor's own judgment in a trial (first or second instance).

cards.q: Which structural parallels exist between a RESCRIPTUM and a preliminary ruling of the CJEU? (Kontrollfrage)
cards.a:
Both answer a legal question put by another body; the concrete case is then decided by someone else on that basis.
• Rescript: emperor answers the query on the reported facts → the judge decides if the facts are proven.
• Art 267 TFEU: CJEU answers the question of EU law → the national body decides the case.

cards.q: How did the function of rescripts change after the final redaction of the edict?
cards.a: At first they interpreted existing law for the individual case; afterwards they increasingly created law and were observed beyond the concrete case.

cards.q: Distinguish the chanceries AB EPISTULIS and A LIBELLIS.
cards.a:
AB EPISTULIS handled queries from officials; A LIBELLIS handled queries from private persons.
• Often headed by important jurists — but the emperor had the last word.

cards.q: Who could ask the emperor for a rescript?
cards.a: Officials or private persons, asking for the emperor's legal opinion on the facts they reported.

9.title: Part 1 as a toolkit for exegesis — review
9.text: Gamauf's Part 1 contains no model exegesis, but its content gives several tools you will use when commenting a Digest text. (1) LEGAL LAYER of the remedy or institution: when a text mentions the REI VINDICATIO you are in IUS CIVILE (civil ownership); the ACTIO PUBLICIANA belongs to IUS HONORARIUM (bonitary ownership); an ACTIO IN FACTUM or ACTIO UTILIS signals praetorian extension of a civil remedy (e.g. of the LEX AQUILIA). MANCIPATIO and USUCAPIO are ius civile, TRADITIO and OCCUPATIO ius gentium. (2) HYPOTHETICAL CHARACTER of the answer: both a jurist's RESPONSUM and an imperial RESCRIPT solve a LEGAL QUESTION on the facts as reported, not a real case; they help a party only if those facts are proven. This is why an exegesis states the relevant facts and the legal question before the answer (developed in Part 2). (3) DATING: the classical period (end of 1st c. BC – 3rd c. AD), the EDICTUM PERPETUUM (c. 130 AD) and the end of praetorian law-making help you place a jurist and his work. The four Kontrollfragen of Part 1 (purposes of the Twelve Tables; adapting private law in the Republic; force of law of the oratio principis; rescript vs CJEU preliminary ruling) are covered by cards in sections 4, 6, 7 and 8.

cards.q: A Digest text mentions the ACTIO PUBLICIANA. Which legal layer are you in, and what does it protect?
cards.a: IUS HONORARIUM — it protects BONITARY ownership (as opposed to civil ownership protected by the REI VINDICATIO of the ius civile).

cards.q: What does it tell you when the praetor grants an ACTIO IN FACTUM or ACTIO UTILIS in a text?
cards.a: Praetorian AD HOC protection beyond the wording of the edict or civil law — IUS HONORARIUM supplementing the ius civile (e.g. actiones in factum to the LEX AQUILIA).

cards.q: Why must the facts a jurist relies on be proven before a party can use his RESPONSUM (or a RESCRIPT)?
cards.a: Because the jurist (or emperor) answered only the LEGAL QUESTION on the facts as reported in the query, not a real case; the judge follows the answer only if those facts are proven.
